passage: The Class 4 room smelled of chalk and wet umbrellas. Ma'am pinned up a picture of the colony market and asked, "How many cycles are parked outside the sweet shop?" Vasudha counted. Five. She counted again, touching each one with her eyes. Five. "Four!" said Parul from the front bench, and her friends nodded. "Four, ma'am." Hands shot up for four, one after another. Last week, when Vasudha had said "Mars" instead of "Jupiter", the back row had giggled for the whole period. Her cheeks still remembered it. Slowly her hand went up with the rest. "Four," she mumbled. Ma'am turned the picture towards the window light. "Count again, everyone." Vasudha stared at the fifth cycle, half hidden behind a fruit cart, and wished her hand had stayed down.

qa.q: How many cycles did Vasudha count outside the sweet shop?
qa.a: Vasudha counted five cycles, and counted again to be sure.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha raise her hand for four even though she had counted five?
qa.a: She was afraid of being laughed at again, because the back row had giggled the whole period when she said "Mars" last week.

qa.q: At the moment the hands went up, what choice could Vasudha have made instead?
qa.a: She could have said she counted five and pointed to the cycle behind the fruit cart, risking a few giggles but trusting her own eyes.

qa.q: How might Parul feel when ma'am asks everyone to count again?
qa.a: Parul might feel unsure and a little embarrassed, realising her quick answer made half the class copy it without checking.

grounding: A child copies the class's wrong answer although she can see the right one, because she fears being laughed at.

passage:
"Bhaiya, can I ask you something?" Aparna dropped her bag by the sofa.
"If it's quick. I've got tuition," Akash said.
"Today Sir asked which bean plant on the window was tallest. Everyone said the blue pot."
"So?"
"The red pot was taller. I could see it. It was touching the grill."
"Then why do you look like you lost a match?"
"Because I said blue too." She pulled at her sock. "Everyone was saying blue. If I said red alone, Kunal would call me Miss Red Pot for a month."
Akash sat down next to her. "Did Sir measure?"
"Tomorrow. With a scale."
"And if it's red?"
"Then I was right and I said the wrong thing." She groaned into a cushion. "Why did my mouth do that?"

qa.q: Which pot did Aparna see was taller?
qa.a: The red pot was taller; it was touching the grill.

qa.q: What was Aparna worried about when she said blue with everyone else?
qa.a: She worried that Kunal would call her Miss Red Pot for a month if she said red alone 😰

qa.q: When Sir measures tomorrow, what could Aparna choose to say?
qa.a: She could tell Sir she saw the red pot touching the grill and should have said so, a small way to stand by what she saw.

qa.q: How does Akash seem to see his sister's choice, judging from his questions?
qa.a: Akash doesn't scold; he sits beside her and asks whether Sir measured, as if helping her notice that the truth will come out anyway.

grounding: A child follows the class's answer though she can see it is wrong, because disagreeing alone risks being teased.

passage: Last year, in Class 3, our quiz team had to write one answer on the slate: how many legs does a spider have? I knew it was eight. I had counted them on the spider behind our bathroom door. But Kavitha said, "Six, obviously," and the other three said, "Yes, six." Then they all looked at me, because I was holding the chalk. My face got hot. If I said eight and was wrong, they would laugh the way they laughed when I read "island" as "is-land". So I wrote 6. We lost the point. On the way home I told Kavitha, "I knew it was eight." Kavitha stopped walking. "Then why didn't you say, Shalini?" I didn't have an answer. I still think about that chalk.

qa.q: How many legs did Shalini know a spider has?
qa.a: Shalini knew it was eight, from counting the legs on the spider behind the bathroom door.

qa.q: What was Shalini afraid of when the team looked at the chalk?
qa.a: Shalini was afraid of being laughed at for saying eight, the way the class laughed at "is-land".

qa.q: Which moment was the real choice for Shalini, and what could Shalini have done there?
qa.a: The choice came with the chalk in hand; Shalini could have said, "I counted them, it's eight," before writing anything.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel on hearing "I knew it was eight" on the walk home?
qa.a: Kavitha might feel surprised and a bit let down that a point was lost when a teammate knew the answer all along.

grounding: A child writes the group's wrong answer despite knowing the truth, because disagreeing alone feels risky.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 3, Thursday. Written by Jaya Ma'am.

In today's quick-quiz I asked, "Which is heavier: one kilo of cotton or one kilo of iron?" Rohit shouted, "Iron!" and the whole row repeated it. Jasleen, eight, sat very still. I saw her whisper "same" to herself and start writing it on her slate. Then she looked around at everyone saying iron. She rubbed out "same" with her sleeve and wrote "iron". When a boy laughed at Manu for a wrong answer earlier, Jasleen had laughed too, and I think she remembered it. At break she came to my desk and asked quietly, "Ma'am, is it the same?" I said yes. She looked at her grey sleeve.

What I did next: from tomorrow, children will write answers on their slates privately before anyone speaks.

qa.q: What did Jasleen first write on her slate?
qa.a: She started writing 'same' on her slate.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen rub out her answer?
qa.a: She was worried about being laughed at for being the only one to disagree, since the whole row was saying iron and she had seen Manu laughed at.

qa.q: Why is the teacher's new rule a good step?
qa.a: Writing answers privately before anyone speaks lets children like Jasleen keep their own answer without feeling the pressure of the group.

qa.q: How might Manu feel about quiz time after being laughed at earlier?
qa.a: Manu may feel nervous and embarrassed, and less willing to answer aloud, just as the laughter made Jasleen afraid to disagree.

grounding: An eight-year-old knows the right answer but switches to the group's wrong answer because disagreeing alone feels risky.

passage:
Saturday

Scouts map day. We had to find the old well using the map and a compass. Joseph was holding the map and said, "The stream goes this way, towards the hill." Everyone said, "Yes, yes, hill." I looked at the compass. The needle said the stream was going the other way. I was nearly sure.

But Joseph is the patrol leader, and all five of them were already walking. If I said "wrong way" and I was wrong, they'd call me Compass Girl for the whole camp. So I walked behind them and didn't say anything.

We walked for twenty minutes and ended up at a cow shed. Then Joseph turned the map around and went red. We went back the way I thought.

Nobody knew I had known. I feel stupid for being right and quiet.

- Gurleen

qa.q: Where did the patrol end up after walking for twenty minutes?
qa.a: They ended up at a cow shed.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen keep quiet even though the compass showed the other way?
qa.a: She was afraid that if she spoke alone and was wrong, the others would tease her and call her Compass Girl for the whole camp.

qa.q: What could Gurleen try next time she is nearly sure the group is wrong?
qa.a: She could quietly show Joseph the compass and ask Joseph to check, which is less scary than announcing that everyone is wrong.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel on learning Gurleen had known the right way?
qa.a: Joseph might feel embarrassed but also wish she had spoken, since it would have saved the whole patrol twenty minutes.

grounding: A ten-year-old sees the compass contradict the group but follows everyone, worried about being laughed at if she disagrees alone.
